title: AI Policy & Tools for Government Workers

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

If you work for a government agency, the AI landscape you navigate is different from the consumer landscape covered in the rest of this course — not because government AI is less capable, but because procurement, security categorization, and rapidly shifting agency policy all sit on top of it. Mid-2026 has been an especially volatile stretch: sweeping OMB guidance accelerating AI adoption, a governmentwide marketplace of deeply discounted enterprise AI deals, a dedicated GSA testing platform, and — in a genuinely disruptive turn — a Pentagon national-security designation that triggered several agencies to drop a major AI vendor within weeks. This lesson gives you the practical map: what's actually authorized, why you can't just use your personal ChatGPT account for work, and how to find out — and document — what's sanctioned at your own workplace.

## The Policy Backbone — OMB M-25-21 and M-25-22

Two OMB memoranda, both issued April 3, 2025, set the framework nearly every federal AI policy you'll encounter traces back to.

**M-25-21, "Accelerating Federal Use of AI through Innovation, Governance, and Public Trust,"** replaced the prior administration's M-24-10 and directs agencies around three priorities: innovation, governance, and public trust. Concretely, it required every executive agency to name a Chief AI Officer within 60 days, and to publish an agency-wide AI Strategy within 180 days. It also collapsed the older "rights-impacting" and "safety-impacting" categories into a single **"high-impact AI"** designation, requiring agencies to bring every high-impact system into compliance — or shut it down — by April 15, 2026.

**M-25-22, "Driving Efficient Acquisition of Artificial Intelligence in Government,"** issued the same day, governs how agencies actually buy AI: fostering competition among vendors, tracking AI performance once acquired, and requiring cross-functional review before purchase. It applies to any AI contract solicited on or after September 30, 2025.

More recent guidance keeps building on this foundation: **M-26-04** ("Increasing Public Trust in Artificial Intelligence Through Unbiased AI Principles," December 11, 2025) and **M-26-05** ("Adopting a Risk-based Approach to Software and Hardware Security," January 23, 2026). The practical upshot for you as an employee: your agency should have a published AI Strategy and a named Chief AI Officer by now, and both are the right starting points when you want to know what's actually approved.

## GSA's OneGov Deals and USAi.gov

In August 2025, GSA added OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude, and Google's Gemini to its Multiple Award Schedule under a program called **OneGov**, negotiating strikingly cheap governmentwide pricing: ChatGPT Enterprise for $1 per agency for a year, Claude for Enterprise and Claude for Government for $1 across the executive, legislative, and judicial branches, and Gemini for Government for 47 cents per agency for a year (through 2026). Claude for Government specifically supports FedRAMP High workloads, meaning it's authorized for more sensitive unclassified work than a standard commercial tier.

**USAi.gov** is GSA's own governmentwide sandbox — a unified chatbot interface, API, and management console where agencies can test major models (from OpenAI, Google, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft, xAI, and, with the exception noted below, Anthropic) before committing to a full procurement. Fifteen agencies were using it as of April 2026, though GSA has announced it will move to a cost-recoverable (paid) model for agencies starting in fiscal year 2027 rather than remaining free.

The product names above — ChatGPT Gov, Claude for Government, Gemini for Government — are the actual government-specific tiers, distinct from the consumer products of the same name, and they're the tools your agency is actually authorized to run under contract, if it has adopted them.

## Why Approved Tools Can Change Overnight — The Anthropic Case

Government AI approval status is more volatile than you might assume, and a concrete 2026 episode makes the point vividly. On February 27, 2026, the Pentagon designated Anthropic a "supply chain risk to national security" — a label previously reserved for companies like Huawei and ZTE. Anthropic disputes the designation's legal basis and filed federal lawsuits on March 9, 2026; a federal judge granted a preliminary injunction blocking the designation on March 26, 2026, after Microsoft filed an amicus brief supporting Anthropic. The dispute remains unresolved as of this writing.

In the weeks after the designation, several agencies moved fast: the State Department migrated its internal chatbot from Claude to GPT-4.1, Treasury and Health & Human Services began dropping Claude in favor of ChatGPT or Gemini, and the Office of Personnel Management removed Claude from its approved use-case list (adding xAI's Grok and OpenAI's Codex instead). The Senate approved ChatGPT, Gemini, and Microsoft Copilot for staff use but did not approve Claude — even though the House of Representatives had approved Claude back in September 2024. Meanwhile the Department of Defense has continued awarding contracts to Anthropic, Google, OpenAI, and xAI alike, and reportedly authorized Grok and Gemini for use in classified systems.

The point isn't which company is right — it's what this reveals about the ground you're standing on: **an AI tool your agency approved last quarter may not be approved this quarter**, for reasons that have nothing to do with the tool's quality and everything to do with a fast-moving national security or contracting decision made well above your level. Checking current status before you rely on any tool for real work isn't excessive caution — it's the only way to stay compliant in an environment this fluid.

## Why You Can't Just Use Your Personal ChatGPT Account for Work

Every reason below is a real constraint, not bureaucratic caution for its own sake:

**Data handling and training.** A personal consumer account's terms of service typically allow the provider to use your conversations to improve its models unless you've specifically opted out — completely unacceptable for anything containing Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI), personally identifiable information (PII), procurement-sensitive data, or pre-decisional deliberations. Government-specific tiers (ChatGPT Gov, Claude for Government, Gemini for Government) are contracted with different data handling terms specifically because of this.

**Security authorization boundaries.** FedRAMP authorization (Moderate, High) is granted to a specific product configuration under a specific contract — not to "ChatGPT" or "Claude" as a brand name. Your personal login isn't running inside that authorized boundary, even if it's technically "the same model."

**Procurement and accountability.** M-25-22 exists precisely so agencies can track what AI is actually in use, at what cost, and with what risk profile. A personal account is invisible to that tracking — if something goes wrong, there's no contract, no audit trail, and no vendor accountability your agency can invoke.

**The practical rule:** if your agency has an approved, contracted AI tool, use that account, through that access path, for anything related to your job. Save personal accounts for genuinely personal use, on your own time, with your own data.

## Approved-Use vs. Personal-Use: The Day-to-Day Line

Most confusion isn't about big strategic questions — it's about small daily choices. A few concrete patterns:

- **Drafting a public-facing memo using your agency's approved ChatGPT Gov / Claude for Government / Gemini for Government account:** almost always fine, subject to your normal review process.
- **Pasting a constituent's case file, a procurement-sensitive draft, or any CUI into a personal AI account to "just get a quick summary":** not fine, regardless of how good the summary is — this is exactly the data-handling risk described above.
- **Using USAi.gov to test how a model handles a hypothetical, non-sensitive version of a task before deciding whether to request full access:** exactly what USAi.gov is for.
- **Using your personal phone's AI assistant or a personal account to check personal email during a break:** personal use, no agency policy implication, use freely.

When in doubt, the test isn't "is this a good AI tool" — it's "is this specific account, under this specific contract, authorized for this specific kind of data." Your agency's Chief AI Officer or your IT security office is the authority on that question, not general reputation or how well the tool performed for you elsewhere.

**USAi.gov is designed for exactly this kind of exploration.** If you want to try a model before requesting formal access, or compare how two approved tools handle the same non-sensitive task, USAi.gov's unified interface is the sanctioned way to do it — no separate procurement required, though GSA has signaled agencies will start paying for it starting in fiscal year 2027.

**Check before you rely, every time.** As the Anthropic episode shows, an agency's list of approved AI tools can change within weeks for reasons entirely outside your control. Before using any AI tool for real work — not personal curiosity — confirm its current status with your agency's published AI use-case inventory or your Chief AI Officer's office, even if it was approved last month.

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Identify What's Actually Sanctioned at Your Workplace
sections.content:
This workshop produces a real, verified answer for your specific workplace — not a guess based on what you've heard secondhand.

**Step 1 — Find your agency's published AI Strategy and the name of your Chief AI Officer** (required under M-25-21). Check your agency's public website, your intranet, or ask your IT or security office if you can't locate it.

**Step 2 — Check whether your agency has adopted any of the OneGov-discounted tools** (ChatGPT Enterprise/Gov, Claude for Enterprise/Government, Gemini for Government) or provides access via USAi.gov.

**Step 3 — List every AI tool you currently use for any work task**, however minor — drafting an email, summarizing a document, researching a topic.

**Step 4 — For each tool on your list, determine: personal account, or agency-sanctioned account?** If you're not sure, that uncertainty is the whole point of this exercise — find out, don't guess.

**Step 5 — Flag anything you found that's a personal account being used for work content containing PII, CUI, or procurement-sensitive information.** These need to stop immediately, not just get noted for later.

**Step 6 — Write down the real answer for your workplace**: which tools are approved, through which access path, for which kinds of data.

**Outcome:** a real, verified list of sanctioned versus unsanctioned AI use at your actual workplace — the foundation for Workshop 2.

sections.question: You've been using your personal ChatGPT account to summarize an interagency planning document that contains procurement-sensitive details. A colleague says this is fine because "it's the same ChatGPT either way." What's wrong with that reasoning?
options: Nothing — if the model is the same, the account used to access it doesn't matter

A personal consumer account's terms of service typically allow the provider to use conversations to improve its models, and a personal login doesn't run inside any FedRAMP-authorized boundary or contract — the agency-sanctioned tier (e.g., ChatGPT Gov) exists specifically to avoid this
It's only a problem if the document is classified, not merely procurement-sensitive
It's fine as long as you don't paste the document title into the chat
sections.explanation: "Same underlying model" doesn't mean "same authorized boundary." FedRAMP authorization and a government-specific contract (like ChatGPT Gov) cover a particular product configuration and particular data-handling terms — a personal consumer account has neither. Procurement-sensitive information doesn't need to be classified to be inappropriate for a personal AI account; CUI and procurement-sensitive data are exactly the categories government-specific AI tiers were contracted to handle safely. Removing the document title doesn't change what's in the body of the content you pasted.

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Draft a One-Page Approved-Use Note for Your Team
sections.content:
Using what you found in Workshop 1, turn it into something your team can actually use.

**Step 1 — Draft a one-page, plain-language note** titled something like "AI Tools — What's Approved for Our Team."

**Step 2 — Include, specifically:**
- Which AI tools are approved, and through what access path (your agency-sanctioned login — never a personal account)
- What kinds of data are never allowed in any AI tool, regardless of which one (CUI, PII, procurement-sensitive information, pre-decisional deliberations)
- Who to contact with questions (your Chief AI Officer's office or your IT security contact)
- A note that this list can change quickly, and where to check for the current version

**Step 3 — Ask Claude** (through your agency-sanctioned account if you have access, or generally if you don't yet): *"Review this one-page AI use note for a government team [paste your draft]. What's missing? Is anything unclear to someone with no security background?"*

**Step 4 — Share the draft with your supervisor or team lead before circulating it as anything official.** This is guidance you're personally offering, not agency policy, unless your organization has specifically designated you to write policy — say so explicitly in the note if that's the case.

**Step 5 — Save the final version somewhere your team will actually see it** (a shared drive, a team channel, a printed copy near the coffee machine — whatever people will actually read).

**Outcome:** a real, one-page reference document grounded in your workplace's actual approved tools, not generic advice — something your team can consult the next time they're unsure whether a tool is fine to use.

sections.question: You've finished drafting your one-page approved-use note for your team. What's the most important step before you circulate it?
options: Publish it immediately — any accurate information about approved tools is better than none, and speed matters most

Have your supervisor or team lead review it first, since you likely don't have the authority to declare official policy, and approved-tool status can shift quickly enough that even accurate information can go stale
Add your own name as the agency's official Chief AI Officer so people take it seriously
Skip review — since you personally verified the tools in Workshop 1, no further check is needed
sections.explanation: The note is genuinely useful, but it's personal guidance, not official agency policy — sharing it as though it were policy without a supervisor's review risks stating something inaccurately or overstepping your actual authority. Given how quickly approved-tool status has shifted in 2026 (the Anthropic episode being the clearest example), a second set of eyes and a clear "check for updates" note both matter more than speed. Claiming a title you don't hold (option C) would be actively misleading, and skipping review (option D) ignores that your own verification, however careful, isn't the same as institutional sign-off.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 13-6.** You now understand the policy backbone (OMB's M-25-21 and M-25-22, and their 2025-2026 follow-ons), the GSA OneGov deals and USAi.gov sandbox, and why government-specific AI tiers (ChatGPT Gov, Claude for Government, Gemini for Government) exist as distinct products from their consumer namesakes. You've seen how fast approved-tool status can change — the Anthropic supply-chain-risk episode being the clearest 2026 example — and why that means checking current status matters more than trusting last quarter's approval. You've identified what's actually sanctioned at your own workplace and drafted a real one-page note your team can use.

**Across industries:**
- Healthcare: A hospital IT team faces the same approved-tool volatility this lesson describes — a vendor's healthcare data-handling agreement can change status abruptly, so clinicians must recheck the current approved-tools list rather than assume last quarter's approval still holds.
- Financial-Systems Analyst: A bank's model-risk-management team treats an AI vendor's compliance certification the way this lesson treats FedRAMP authorization — tied to a specific contracted configuration, not a brand name, and subject to sudden revocation.
- Education: A school district's approved AI vendor list must be checked before a teacher uses a personal account on a student's confidential record — the same personal-account-vs-sanctioned-account line this lesson draws for CUI.
- Legal: A law firm's approved AI tools for privileged client material shift when a vendor's data-handling terms change, mirroring how a federal agency dropped an approved tool from its use-case list within weeks.
- Nonprofit: A nonprofit receiving federal grant funding inherits procurement-tracking obligations similar to M-25-22 when it uses AI tools on federally funded program data, even though it isn't itself a federal agency.
